newsitem.title: TOGO: Symbolic handshake by Zaire warring parties - Togo.
newsitem.headline: Symbolic handshake by Zaire warring parties - Togo.

text.p: Zaire's warring parties, brought together by Organisation of African Unity (OAU) leaders in an attempt to broker peace, shook hands in a symbolic first step towards reconciliation, host Togo said.

Togo's Foreign Minister Pierre Koffi Panou told Radio France International that the handshake between representatives of the two sides took place late on Wednesday on the sidelines of a special OAU summit on the crisis at the heart of Africa.

But with Laurent Kabila's rebels having the upper hand on the battlefield and their representatives at the summit repeatedly stressing that they were not in Togo to negotiate, any more significant breakthrough looked unlikely.
"It's a very important stage which has been crossed. Here you have foes who were not speaking to one another who shook hands," Panou said.
He described the handshake, during a private meeting hosted by Togo's president, Gnassingbe Eyadema, as "a very strong signal for all the main players and the international community".
The rebels, who have been fighting to topple veteran President Mobutu Sese Seko since October, were attending their first major international forum.
Earlier, the heads of state brought the two sides together in the same room during a closed session of their summit and allowed each to have their say.
"They were brought in. Both sides explained their position in front of everyone," one source told Reuters.

But one senior African delegate suggested that the fact that the rebels were allowed to address Wednesday's closed session of the summit had angered the delegation from Zaire's central authorities, who listened under protest.

Rwanda had suggested that the rebel delegates be allowed to address the closed session but the delegation from Kinshasa had expected more informal contacts on the sidelines of the formal summit, he added.
Throughout the meeting, the rebel team has insisted it is not in Togo to negotiate.

"We are not here to negotiate," Gaetab Kakudji, one of the two Kabila representatives told Reuters after U.N. Secretary- General Kofi Annan and OAU Secretary-General Salim Ahmed Salim both called for the fighting to stop and talks to start.
Salim described the presence of the two sides in Togo's capital Lome as a "unique opportunity to move the peace process forward" and urged them to seize it.
"I wish, in the name of Africa, to appeal to both parties to rise to the challenge of the hour," he said.
"The fighting must stop and dialogue must begin," Annan told delegates. "Military might or intervention alone cannot successfully lay the foundations for a lasting peace."

France and the United States, among Western nations who have sent troops to the region to evacuate their nationals if peace efforts collapse and violence erupts in Kinshasa, have been jointly lobbying for a truce and talks.
Diplomatic pressure focused on a five point peace plan formulated by U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun, who was also attending the summit.
Heads of state and other would-be mediators all urged the rebels to embrace the plan, which has already been accepted by the government in Kinshasa.
In Kinshasa itself, political confusion reigned after he resignation of Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo's government. Kengo remains in charge in a caretaker capacity.
The central authorities in Kinshasa are represented by Foreign Minister Kamanda wa Kamdana and the deputy speaker of the transitional assembly, Andre Boboliko.
